CHAPTER LXXV

Clement sighed. He began to doubt whether he had taken the wisest course
with a creature so passionate.

But young as he was, he had already learned many lessons of
ecclesiastical wisdom. For one thing he had been taught to pause, ie.,
in certain difficulties, neither to do nor to say anything, until the
matter should clear itself a little.

He therefore held his peace and prayed for wisdom.

All he did was gently to withdraw his foot.

But his penitent flung her arms round it with a piteous cry, and held it
convulsively, and wept over it.

And now the agony of shame, as well as penitence, she was in, showed
itself by the bright red that crept over her very throat, as she lay
quivering at his feet.

“My daughter,” said Clement gently, “take courage. Torment thyself no
more about this Gerard, who is not. As for me, I am Brother Clement,
whom Heaven hath sent to thee this day to comfort thee, and help thee
save thy soul. Thou last made me thy confessor, I claim, then, thine
obedience.”

“Oh, yes,” sobbed the penitent.

“Leave this pilgrimage, and instant return to Rome. Penitence abroad is
little worth. There where we live lie the temptations we must defeat, or
perish; not fly in search of others more showy, but less lethal. Easy to
wash the feet of strangers, masked ourselves, Hard to be merely meek and
charitable with those about us.”

“I'll never, never lay finger on her again.”

“Nay, I speak not of servants only, but of dependents, kinsmen, friends.
This be thy penance; the last thing at night, and the first thing after
matins, call to mind thy sin, and God His goodness; and so be humble and
gentle to the faults of those around thee. The world it courts the rich;
but seek thou the poor: not beggars; these for the most are neither
honest nor truly poor. But rather find out those who blush to seek thee,
yet need thee sore. Giving to them shalt lend to Heaven. Marry a good
son of the Church.”

“Me? I will never marry.”

“Thou wilt marry within the year. I do entreat and command thee to marry
one that feareth God. For thou art very clay. Mated ill thou shalt be
naught. But wedding a worthy husband thou mayest, Dei gratia, live a
pious princess; ay, and die a saint.”

“I?”

“Thou.”

He then desired her to rise and go about the good work he had set her.

She rose to her knees, and removing her mask, cast an eloquent look upon
him, then lowered her eyes meekly.

“I will obey you as I would an angel. How happy I am, yet unhappy; for
oh, my heart tells me I shall never look on you again. I will not go
till I have dried your feet.”

“It needs not. I have excused thee this bootless penance.”

“'Tis no penance to me. Ah! you do not forgive me, if you will not let
me dry your poor feet.”

“So be it then,” said Clement resignedly; and thought to himself,
“Levius quid foemina.”

But these weak creatures, that gravitate towards the small, as heavenly
bodies towards the great, have yet their own flashes of angelic
intelligence.

When the princess had dried the friar's feet, she looked at him with
tears in her beautiful eyes, and murmured with singular tenderness and
goodness--

“I will have masses said for her soul. May I?” she added timidly.

This brought a faint blush into the monk's cheek, and moistened his cold
blue eye. It came so suddenly from one he was just rating so low.

“It is a gracious thought,” he said. “Do as thou wilt: often such acts
fall back on the doer like blessed dew. I am thy confessor, not hers;
thine is the soul I must now do my all to save, or woe be to my own. My
daughter, my dear daughter, I see good and ill angels fighting for thy
soul this day, ay, this moment; oh, fight thou on thine own side. Dost
thou remember all I bade thee?”

“Remember!” said the princess. “Sweet saint, each syllable of thine is
graved in my heart.”

“But one word more, then. Pray much to Christ, and little to his
saints.”

“I will.”

“And that is the best word I have light to say to thee. So part we on
it. Thou to the place becomes thee best, thy father's house, I to my
holy mother's work.”

“Adieu,” faltered the princess. “Adieu, thou that I have loved too well,
hated too ill, known and revered too late; forgiving angel, adieu--for
ever.”

The monk caught her words, though but faltered in a sigh.

“For ever?” he cried aloud, with sudden ardour. “Christians live 'for
ever,' and love 'for ever,' but they never part 'for ever. They part, as
part the earth and sun, to meet more brightly in a little while. You and
I part here for life. And what is our life? One line in the great story
of the Church, whose son and daughter we are; one handful in the sand of
time, one drop in the ocean of 'For ever.' Adieu--for the little moment
called 'a life!' We part in trouble, we shall meet in peace: we part
creatures of clay, we shall meet immortal spirits: we part in a world of
sin and sorrow, we shall meet where all is purity and love divine; where
no ill passions are, but Christ is, and His saints around Him clad in
white. There, in the turning of an hour-glass, in the breaking of a
bubble, in the passing of a cloud, she, and thou, and I, shall meet
again; and sit at the feet of angels and archangels, apostles and
saints, and beam like them with joy unspeakable, in the light of the
shadow of God upon His throne, FOR EVER--AND EVER--AND EVER.”

And so they parted. The monk erect, his eyes turned heavenwards and
glowing with the sacred fire of zeal; the princess slowly retiring and
turning more than once to cast a lingering glance of awe and tender
regret on that inspired figure.

She went home subdued, and purified. Clement, in due course, reached
Basle, and entered on his duties, teaching in the University, and
preaching in the town and neighbourhood. He led a life that can be
comprised in two words; deep study, and mortification. My reader has
already a peep into his soul. At Basle he advanced in holy zeal and
knowledge.

The brethren of his order began to see in him a descendant of the saints
and martyrs.

One such lesson was patience—knowing when to remain silent, to say nothing and do nothing, until the turmoil of the soul might settle into clarity. So he said nothing. Instead, he prayed for guidance.

All he did was gently withdraw his foot from where it rested. But the penitent clutched it at once, her arms winding tightly around it as she sobbed aloud, her body trembling beneath the weight of her sorrow. A deep flush rose up her neck and spread across her face, betraying not only shame but the fierce struggle within. She lay before him, quivering like a leaf in the wind.

“Daughter,” he said softly, “take heart. Do not torment yourself further over this Gerard, who is no more. I am Brother Clement—sent by Heaven today to comfort you, to help you save your soul. You made me your confessor; therefore, I claim your obedience.”

“Oh, yes,” she wept, her voice breaking. “Leave this pilgrimage, and return at once to Rome. Penitence far from home is little worth. The true trials are those we must face where we live—not fleeing to distant lands in search of grander sins, but enduring the daily temptations that surround us. It is easy to wash the feet of strangers when we wear masks. But how hard it is to be gentle, truly humble, with those we know and love.”

“I will never touch her again,” she vowed.

“No,” he replied, “I speak not only of servants, but of all who depend on you—kinsmen, friends, even family. This shall be your penance: each night before sleep, and each morning after matins, remember your sin and God’s mercy. Let that memory soften your heart and make you kinder to others’ faults. The world honors wealth, but seek instead the poor—not beggars, for most are neither honest nor truly destitute. Rather, find those who blush to ask for help, yet need it dearly. Give to them, and you lend to Heaven itself. Marry a good son of the Church.”

“Me?” she whispered. “I will never marry.”

“You will marry within the year,” he declared firmly. “And I command you—to wed one who fears God. For you are fragile clay. A bad match will break you. But if you choose well, through God’s grace, you may live as a pious princess—and die a saint.”

“I?” she murmured.

“You.”

He then asked her to rise and go forth to fulfill the task he had set before her. She knelt slowly, removed her veil, and looked up at him with eyes full of unspoken emotion. Then, lowering her gaze in humility, she said, “I will obey you as I would an angel. How happy I am—and yet how sad! For my heart tells me I shall never see you again. I will not leave until I have dried your feet.”

“It is unnecessary,” he said gently. “I have absolved you of this useless act.”

“But it is no burden to me,” she insisted. “Ah, you do not forgive me—if you refuse to let me tend to your feet.”

“Very well,” Clement said, yielding with quiet resignation. And inwardly he thought, *Levius quid foemina.* Yet even such frail beings, drawn to small things as stars are drawn to the sun, sometimes shine with sudden flashes of divine insight.

When she had finished drying his feet, she looked up at him again, tears glistening in her eyes, and whispered with tender compassion, “I will have masses said for her soul. May I?”

The words struck him like a soft blow. A faint blush touched his cheek, and a single tear moistened his cold blue eye. It came from one whom he had just spoken to with sternness, yet now offered such grace.

“It is a noble thought,” he replied. “Do as you wish. Such deeds often return to bless the giver like dew upon dry earth. I am your confessor, not hers. My duty is to save your soul—or else suffer the consequences. My daughter, my dear daughter, I see now angels fighting for your soul—good and evil—this very moment. Stand firm on your side. Do you remember all I have told you?”

“Remember?” she echoed. “Sweet saint, every word you spoke is carved into my heart.”

“One last thing,” he said. “Pray much to Christ, and little to His saints.”

“I will.”

“And that,” he added, “is the best counsel I can give you. So let us part on this.” He paused. “You to the place most fitting—your father’s house. I to my holy mother’s work.”

“Adieu,” she breathed, barely audible.

“Adieu,” he answered, “you whom I loved too deeply, hated too fiercely, known and honored too late. Forgiving angel, adieu—for ever.”

He heard her words, though spoken only in a sigh. “For ever?” he called out, his voice rising with sudden fervor. “Christians live for ever, and love for ever—but they never part for ever. They separate, as earth and sun do, only to meet again in greater light. We part here for life. And what is life? One line in the great story of the Church—of which we are both children. One grain in the sand of time, one drop in the ocean of eternity. Adieu—for this brief moment called ‘a life.’ We part in sorrow, we shall meet in peace. We part as mortal creatures, we shall meet as immortal spirits. We part in a world of sin and pain, we shall meet in a realm of purity and divine love, where no darkness remains, only Christ, and His saints robed in white. There—in the turn of an hourglass, in the burst of a bubble, in the passing of a cloud—we shall meet again. And sit at the feet of angels and archangels, apostles and saints, radiant with joy beyond words, bathed in the shadow of God upon His throne—FOR EVER—AND EVER—AND EVER.”

And so they parted.

The monk stood tall, his gaze lifted heavenward, burning with sacred fire. The princess walked away slowly, glancing back again and again—each look filled with awe and quiet regret. She returned home subdued, purified, transformed.

Clement reached Basel in due time, and took up his duties: teaching in the university, preaching throughout the town and surrounding villages. His life became defined by two qualities: profound study and rigorous self-denial. The reader has already glimpsed the depth of his soul. In Basel, he grew ever deeper in spiritual zeal and learning. The brothers of his order began to see in him a true heir to the saints and martyrs.
